posts.title: Thinking Partner, Not Thinking Replacement
posts.body:
AI works best as a thinking partner and fails as a thinking replacement, and my college freshman reminded me of that when he called to talk about Copilot.

The call I didn't expect

For years, my son wanted nothing to do with AI. That's a little awkward when your dad leads an AI practice for a living.

When I dropped Declan off at Texas State in August, I wrote about what I hoped college would be for him. I wanted him to learn to think critically, to engage civilly, and to find something worth being absorbed in, then give himself fully to it. So far, he's been giving himself fully to his gaming guild. Warhammer and D&D have his complete devotion. I remain hopeful he'll find something more meaningful. But I'll take the commitment as a sign the capacity is there.

Then, a few weeks ago, he called me. Not about money or laundry or when he was coming home. He wanted to talk about how he was using Copilot.

The kid who'd resisted AI for years, despite (or maybe because of) what his dad does, had found his way there on his own. And he had real questions.

What we talked about

We talked through the different models and what each is best at right now, knowing that "right now" changes every few months. We talked about how to prompt better: giving context, being specific about what you want, and pushing back when the first answer isn't good enough. We talked about how the quality of what you get out depends on the quality of what you put in.

Most of all, we talked about using it as a thinking partner, not a thinking replacement.

That distinction is everything. In August, I wrote that the rarest skill I know is the ability to think, to hold a real position and still listen to someone who holds the opposite one. AI doesn't make that skill obsolete. Used badly, it lets the skill wither. You hand over the hard part and accept whatever comes back. Used well, it makes you sharper. It challenges your first draft, shows you the counterargument you missed, and makes you defend your reasoning.

The same questions in the boardroom

What struck me afterward was how familiar the conversation felt. It's almost exactly the one I've been having with executives across the board. The questions a college freshman asks aren't so different from the ones a leadership team asks. Which tool do I use? How do I get better results? How do I make sure it makes me better instead of lazier?

The answers are the same too. This isn't optional anymore. It's not a trend to wait out or a pilot to run someday. It's here and real, and it's changing how work gets done in classrooms and boardrooms alike.

What to do

The job for all of us, whether we're 19 or 50, is the same: learn to use it for our best outcomes, without outsourcing the thinking that makes us who we are.

Declan, if you're reading this: keep calling. And maybe ask Copilot what else might be worth giving yourself to.

posts.title: When Americans Want Something, They Look to Each Other
posts.body:
Americans still solve problems by looking to each other instead of up the chain, and I saw that instinct at work again recently among business leaders who are trying to make capitalism better.

Look to each other

Alexis de Tocqueville says something in Democracy in America that I think about often (this is my paraphrase, so check the original before you quote me). When the French want something, they ask the government. When the English want something, they ask a lord. When Americans want something, they look to each other and do it themselves.

It was awesome to see that in action recently.

Communities worth showing up for

We have been part of several aligned movements for many years, including Conscious Capitalism, JUST Capital, and Principled Business. We even talk about being a company rooted in the philosophy of Conscious Capitalism.

I believe capitalism has been the greatest force for good (I think the rise of AI will rival it, but that's another post). So whenever I get the opportunity to participate in these communities, I jump on it.

Why I come back energized

It's great to see how many others are interpreting and implementing these principles in service of the markets. That is the Tocqueville instinct applied to business: look to each other, compare notes, and do the work yourselves. I don't think business gets better by waiting for a regulator or a rulebook to hand us better norms. It gets better when peers hold each other to a higher standard and share what is working. I always return energized, knowing there are still many people striving for the betterment of their fellow humans and working to give them the dignity of a meaningful job.

What to do

Find the people near you who are trying to do business better, and go sit in their room. Who are the peers you would look to if you wanted something done, and when did you last show up where they gather?

posts.title: Safe Is the Floor, Not the Goal
posts.body:
An AI product can pass every safety check and still leave people worse at thinking, and most companies only run the first test.

Two different tests

A recent MIT Technology Review op-ed by Sam Hiner and Emma Leiken makes the case at the policy level. Lawmakers are passing industry-backed bills that guard against the worst outcomes (a chatbot that won't encourage self-harm, say), while the quieter damage goes unmeasured. The authors point to MIT research in which young people using ChatGPT to write essays showed weaker brain connectivity, with "cognitive debt" that lingered after the task. The authors' broader argument is that companies can clear those low bars and still build products that quietly change how people think and relate to each other, and that safety should be the minimum, not the finish line. The long-term effects are still being studied, and that work is about teenagers and students. But I keep asking whether our own AI policies do the same thing: define success as "no incident" and call it done.

Start with the floor, then write the ceiling

Step one: look at your internal AI policy and ask what it protects against. Data leakage, bad outputs, and misuse are the floor. Step two: write down what you want people to still be able to do in two years without the tool (draft a client proposal, debug an outage, tell a good idea from a plausible one), and measure that. If it is not written down, it is not measured, and a skill you do not measure is one you can lose without noticing.

Zero incidents is not the same as success

A team with zero incidents and no remaining judgment has not succeeded, it has just not been caught yet. The op-ed's authors put the underlying point well: we build judgment through effort and friction. A tool that removes all of that is making a trade someone should choose on purpose.

What to do

What does your AI policy say about the skills you refuse to lose?
posts.source_text: Watchtower digest (ts 1793639214.073259) built on MIT Technology Review op-ed, 'The focus on AI safety disasters ignores everyday harms' (Hiner and Leiken, 2026-10-26).

posts.title: Your AI Vendor Just Published Its Risk Factors. Have You Read Them?
posts.body:
Anthropic's IPO filing is a rare chance to read what an AI vendor says could go wrong, and your agent's business case should be checked against it before you approve anything.

What the vendor says could go wrong

Most of us pick an AI platform off a demo and a price sheet. On October 26, Anthropic announced it had filed an S-1 with the SEC for a proposed IPO, and the risk factors in a filing like that are a vendor telling investors, in its own words, where the exposure is. I have not read the filing end to end, so what follows comes from VKTR's coverage of the draft, which the Wall Street Journal viewed first. As reported, Anthropic owes roughly $450 billion under cloud agreements, most of which it cannot cancel, and its cloud partners were unwilling to supply all the capacity it asked for. VKTR's read for customers is that a capacity squeeze can show up as rate limits and slower responses. Figures differ across outlets, so check the filing before you quote a number.

The quietest line in your business case

The pricing assumption is usually the quietest line in a business case (and the one nobody revisits). A vendor with large fixed commitments and constrained capacity is a vendor whose terms and service levels can shift, and I read that as a reminder that today's price is not a promise. A workload that is cheap as a pilot can look very different at scale. I wrote about the seat-pricing version of this story in Agents Don't Need Seats. But They Still Cost Money. and this is the cost-side version.

Run the math in private

Read the risk factors of every AI vendor your agents depend on, public or not, and mark which assumptions in your business case are really borrowed from the vendor's current pricing and capacity. Then model a price move in both directions, and a capacity limit, before the agent goes to production. The vendors are doing this math in public now. Your business case should do it in private.

What to do

If your agent's business case only works at today's price, what exactly did you approve?
posts.source_text: Watchtower digest (ts 1793639197.698479) on Anthropic S-1; facts verified against anthropic.com/news/s1-sec and VKTR coverage. Pricing-pressure claim unverified and dropped.

posts.title: Anxiety Is a Supermarket Aisle
posts.body:
('p', 'Anxiety is not the same thing as fear, and much of the AI hesitation I see is anxiety about too many choices, not fear of the technology.')

('h2', 'A soldier in the cereal aisle')

('p', 'Late in The Hurt Locker, a soldier home from Iraq stands in a grocery store staring at a wall of cereal boxes. He survived bombs. What breaks his face is the choice.')

('p', "That scene came to mind when I saw a recent [Free Press conversation between Coleman Hughes and Mark Manson](https://www.thefp.com/p/mark-manson-self-help-anxiety-happiness), which is framed around anxiety as the problem of our age and why war can feel simpler than a supermarket aisle. The full conversation is behind a paywall, so I'm working from its description and my own thinking, not quoting it.")

('p', "The distinction I haven't been able to shake is that fear and anxiety aren't the same thing. Fear has one object. There's a lion, or an emergency, or a hospital to get to, and you move. Anxiety is a pile of imagined outcomes with no clear answer, and the cost of holding them all at once is that you stall. The more paths in front of you, the more you grieve the ones you didn't take (and many of us are exceedingly good at reruns of those untaken paths, ad nauseam).")

('h2', 'What I see in AI conversations')

('p', 'I think that\'s exactly what\'s happening in the AI conversations I\'m close to. (Our teams work inside client environments, and the room is rarely short on options: every vendor, every agent framework, every pilot someone built over a weekend.) The overabundance of choices is the very reason so many people aren\'t moving forward with their own AI adoption. "Where do I start?" is met with a myriad of options, and somebody has to pick one. Nobody is afraid of the technology. They\'re anxious because there are dozens of live decisions and none of them feels safe to make. So they do the safe thing, which is schedule another workshop or just stand still.')

('h2', 'Choosing is a responsibility')

('p', 'My own view is that choosing is a responsibility, and most of us hand it off by collecting good excuses (my parents would be upset, nobody will hire me in this economy, it\'s "their" fault). I\'ve watched leaders do the same with a roadmap. A fifteen-line priority list is an excuse in a nice font.')

('p', "A leader's job here isn't to remove options. It's to collapse the number of live problems to the one that matters this quarter, and to say it out loud so people can finally move. Fear is clarifying. You can borrow some of that clarity without the lion.")

('h2', 'What to do')

('p', 'Count the live problems on your list right now. Which one matters most this quarter, and what are you waiting for before you say it out loud?')

posts.title: We Keep Looking for One Cause
posts.body:
('p', 'Wanting one thing to blame is a reflex, and it fails us with teenagers and with stalled AI programs alike.')

('h2', 'Phones or play')

('p', "Phones or play. That's how the argument about teenagers usually goes, and it's a comfortable one because you get to pick a side.")

('p', "Then I read [a book review in Education Next](https://www.educationnext.org/beyond-play-and-phones-teen-mental-health-book-review-gray-restoring-childhood/) that took apart both sides at once. It covers Peter Gray's Restoring Childhood, which blames the loss of unsupervised play and pushes back on Jonathan Haidt's phone story. The reviewers, Richard Weissbourd and Kiran Bhai, agree play matters. They just don't think any single cause carries the weight. Then they said two things that stopped me. In their surveys, teens aged 12 to 17 are less likely to struggle with anxiety and depression than adults in their twenties and thirties, and young adults are more than twice as likely as teens to. And 34 percent of teens report lacking meaning, purpose, or both, with family life the largest single factor in a kid's mental health.")

('h2', 'The second reflex')

('p', "I have a freshman at Texas State and a youngest who tried something last year that didn't go well. I wrote before about my reflex to [stop the fall](https://driventodevelop.com/2026/08/13/let-them-climb-the-tree/). This review showed me a second reflex: wanting one thing to blame. A phone is easy to blame. So is a school policy. Both give us something to confiscate or something to rail against, and then we feel like we did something. Like we made a difference or progress.")

('p', "I see the same instinct at work. When an AI adoption program stalls, someone wants one root cause. The tool, the training, the vendor, the employee. It's almost never one cause (and the real answer is usually slower and more personal than anyone wants to hear).")

('h2', 'What actually helps')

('p', "What the reviewers land on is hard precisely because it can't be bought: a sturdy relationship with at least one adult, something that feels like meaning, one area where you're good, and the sense that you matter to someone. That list can't be delivered by a rule or a device. It's delivered by showing up, which is the thing I wrote about in [Love With Your Presence](https://driventodevelop.com/2026/10/22/love-with-your-presence/) and still fail at on busy weeks.")

('p', "One caution: I'm quoting a review, and the reviewers have their own view in this fight (both are at Harvard's Graduate School of Education), so read it for yourself and decide how much of the data you trust.")

('h2', 'What to do')

('p', 'If my kid, or someone on my team, were asked to name the adult who steadies them, would they say my name? And if not, what am I too busy fixing?')

posts.title: Would You Write the Same Book in Ten Years?
posts.body:
('p', 'Strong convictions, loosely held only works if you separate the principles that stay from the tactics that change.')

('h2', 'The question about the book')

('p', 'If you rewrote your book in ten years and it came out exactly the same, would you call that consistency or a problem?')

('p', 'Peter Attia was asked something close to that about Outlive, and his answer was that it would worry him. Either he had gotten too rigid, or science had made no progress. That landed differently for me than it would for most readers, because Attia has been a part of my health journey and even part of why I tried rapamycin. I wrote about it in [Health Journey: Healthspan](https://driventodevelop.com/2024/11/22/health-journey-healthspan/), including the videos, the book, and the Sunday dose.')

('p', "So I paid attention when he marked about 400 episodes in [AMA #90](https://peterattiamd.com/ama90/) by walking through positions he has changed. He no longer views metformin as geroprotective for people who are already metabolically healthy. He describes growing uncertainty about rapamycin (I had to ditch it due to side effects myself), which is a strange thing to hear from the guy who pointed you at it. He has also moved away from heavy barbell squats and deadlifts, which made me smile a little, because I've started skipping deadlifts to protect my lower back. A caveat: the full episode is members-only, so I'm working from the free preview and the episode summary.")

('h2', 'Why the loud pivots are harder')

('p', "Notice the difference in how I handled those two. The deadlift I changed with no ceremony. The rapamycin I announced in a post (in part because I had advocated for it), and I suspect that's exactly why revising it feels heavier. I think we run leadership the same way. The call you made out loud at kickoff is the hardest one to walk back, even after the evidence turns, because a pivot can read as drift. So we defend the plan well past its expiration date (and I've watched that cost more than the pivot ever would have).")

('h2', 'Principles versus tactics')

('p', "What I'm taking from Attia is the structure underneath. As the episode summary describes it, the emphasis is on durable principles, strong foundations, and sustainable practices over marginal optimization. For me the principles are short: sleep, move, eat, protect your muscle, and don't hide from the numbers. Deadlifts and rapamycin are tactics. They earned their place for a season, or until they've proven something one way or another.")

('h2', 'What to do')

('p', 'Hold everything loosely and you have no spine. Hold everything tightly and you stop learning. Which call are you defending right now only because you made it out loud?')
